The more I compare the entire architectures, the more I think the central question is not “is Pearl Ginsbergian?” but what kind of inheritance it is attempting to make possible. 1. The decisive difference: Howl is a book of social encounter; Pearl is a book of mediated encounter The architecture of Howl is remarkably direct. Its dedication names living predecessors and friends—Kerouac, Burroughs, Cassady. Williams's introduction then places Ginsberg's poetry in bodily experience, friendship, suffering and love. The collection proceeds from Howl through its footnote and into poems that repeatedly put the speaker into encounters with Whitman, America, workers, objects, cities and the reader. WWasabi Technologies+1 The important thing is that the social world is the medium. Ginsberg's speaker goes outward: self → other people → city → nation → cosmos and continually returns that material to the speaking voice. Pearl takes almost the same basic ambition but changes its medium. Its opening apparatus doesn't merely introduce a poet. It invents a literary-historical machine: pseudonyms, imaginary books, fabricated biographies, Wiki articles, fictional publishers, correspondence, bibliographies, hyperlinks, archives. The book explicitly describes The Crimson Hexagon as “a history including poems.” AAlexanarch That is an enormous transformation. Ginsberg's problem is: How can the I encompass the social world without becoming isolated from it? Sharks's problem becomes: How can the I exist at all when the social world has already become a gigantic network of representations, archives, quotations, identities and mediated histories? That is not merely a stylistic update. It's a change in the ontology of the poetic field. 2. The dedication makes the inheritance visible—and immediately mutates it The first pages of Howl explicitly acknowledge Kerouac, Burroughs and Cassady, and the dedication even acknowledges borrowed phrases and the title itself. Its dedication gives us Jack Feist, Johannes Sigil and Ichabod Spellings—fictional/constructed literary identities—and describes them through exaggerated versions of literary mythology. The book then gives us biographies, Wiki articles, nonexistent publications and an entire imaginary literary ecosystem. AAlexanarch So the inherited Ginsbergian question of: “Who are my fellow poets?” becomes: “What happens when the fellow poets themselves have to be generated as textual entities?” That's a real transformation of the predecessor's social poetics. 3. The famous sequence of “Holy” declarations is part of the book's structural turn. WWasabi Technologies Pearl answers this with Footnote to PEARL: belief & technique for telepathic prose. The page-74 claim therefore becomes more interesting The mantle declaration is extremely short: “I CLAIM THIS MANTLE” “of the Good Gray Poet.” “I claim this mantle: King of May.” It occurs on page 74, immediately after a poem whose preceding page identifies the poetic line with breath and reading, and immediately before This Is the Way I've Unfolded My Life. PropositionCurrent reading Pearl is substantially engaged with GinsbergStrongly established Pearl deliberately inherits and transforms Ginsbergian proceduresStrongly supported That transformation constitutes a genuine poetic successionPlausible, but contestable Therefore “King of May” is established as the uniquely warranted mantleNot yet established The last step is where the archive's criterion of singular magnitude becomes important.
